bio.en: Eric Simons is the co-founder and CEO of StackBlitz, whose AI coding app Bolt became one of the fastest-growing products in history—hitting roughly $20M ARR within two months of launch and approaching $40M—after seven years of building the underlying WebContainer technology.
bio.zh: Eric Simons 是 StackBlitz 的联合创始人兼 CEO；其 AI 编程应用 Bolt 成为史上增长最快的产品之一——上线两个月即达到约 2000 万美元 ARR、并逼近 4000 万美元——而这建立在历时七年打磨的 WebContainer 底层技术之上。

summary.en: Eric tells the story of Bolt as an 'overnight success seven years in the making': StackBlitz was nearly out of money until they realized their browser-based WebContainer tech was perfectly suited for AI products and launched with a single tweet. He credits the small, long-tenured core team as the real engine of their absurd growth, and argues that building technology first and finding the problem later was the right call for them despite conventional wisdom. The conversation is a window into the cutting edge of AI coding tools and where AI-native product building is heading.
summary.zh: Eric 把 Bolt 的故事称为“七年磨一剑的一夜成功”：StackBlitz 一度濒临破产，直到他们意识到自己在浏览器中打造的 WebContainer 技术特别适合 AI 产品，并用一条推文就发布了产品。他把这种惊人的增长归功于一支规模很小、共事多年的核心团队，并主张“先造技术、后找问题”尽管违背常规、对他们却是正确的选择。这期对话是观察 AI 编程工具前沿、以及 AI 原生产品构建走向的一扇窗口。

百分之百是的，没错。我想说的是，这在我看来仍是我们公司最具反向观点的观点之一。多年来，情况一直是这样的。当我们最初……嗯，WebContainer就是我们公司的立足之本。说清楚一点，StackBlitz是一款基于浏览器的深度技术项目，核心问题在于："我们能否开发出基于WebAssembly的操作系统，让它能在浏览器中启动，仅用几百毫秒就能运行完整的开发工具链？"这就是核心目标。（00:20:21）我们最初产生这个想法，是基于这样一个洞察：当我和联合创始人2012年来到硅谷时，我们在芝加哥同街长大，从13岁起就一起写代码。后来我们发现Figma团队早期也曾基于浏览器进行过类似的技术探索。Figma最初的演示Demo甚至不是设计工具，而是展示了在浏览器中模拟水滴落入水面的3D场景。他们的核心论点是：“浏览器新增了WebGL技术（WebAssembly的前身），我们首次有机会开发图形渲染引擎，再在此基础上构建设计工具。但你必须从零开始编写渲染引擎，因为市面上没有现成能编译成WebGL的组件。若想实现所需性能，必然耗时数年。但如果我们成功，必将彻底改变设计领域。” （00:21:00）如今回头看，这一愿景已成现实。2017年，我们发现类似的故事在Web开发和开发环境领域上演：WebAssembly、共享内存、Service Worker等API相继落地。当时我们感叹："理论上能否用WebAssembly编写操作系统，运行Node.js、NPM及全套开发工具链？" （00:22:12）这将彻底改变开发者环境的体验——新手搭建环境总是困难重重。许多人在学习编程时，首要任务并非学习编程本身，而是如何搭建开发环境。加入Netflix等公司后，新人最初几个月都忙于安装运行环境。相较之下，我们设想用户只需点击链接，浏览器就能直接启动环境，简直太棒了。 

（00:22:42）再看真正在Web上成功的生产力应用，如Figma，当你打开文档时，系统并非在云端虚拟机渲染，而是实时使用你的CPU和内存进行处理。Google Docs也是如此。这是唯一能扩展至十亿用户的计算模型。反观早期云IDE，如2009年左右推出的Cloud 9，其核心设计理念是浏览器基本不参与用户请求处理，每个连接用户的环境都是独立运行的。
必须为他们启动一个云虚拟机，然后你的浏览器会接收你的键盘输入，将其发送到服务器，再将处理结果返回。这就是其他所有AI代码、文本转应用程序之类的工具的工作原理。它们全都依赖云虚拟机。（00:23:34）问题在于，小规模应用尚可行，但随着规模扩大，全球甚至连1亿台可租用的云虚拟机都难以满足需求。但全球有数十亿台设备可供运行这些应用。这正是我们在Bolt项目中遇到的挑战——要想打造能大规模扩展的产品，就必须综合考量各方面因素：确保技术能提供最佳体验、零延迟、可控成本。云服务提供免费层级，但随之而来的是服务器被滥用风险，比如用户用服务器挖比特币、发起DDoS攻击等。因此，最终只能收紧政策限制这些行为。但若所有功能都集成在终端设备中，就无需担忧这些问题。

（00:24:18）总之，WebContainer是关键技术。我们花了四五年时间才开发出这款产品。之后数年面临的挑战是如何围绕它构建商业模式。开发者对其赞不绝口，但他们并未愿意为此付费。尽管我内心渴望仅专注于技术创新，但现实告诉我们：我们要打造的是规模化企业。正因如此，项目接近尾声时我们信心倍增，感觉一切都步入正轨。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lot of really interesting lessons from this journey, that I think are counterintuitive. One is, you basically were building a tech first, and then looking for a problem to solve later. Which is often what people tell you not to do. And it worked out, in this case. (00:25:19): The other interesting takeaway here is, it feels like it's a similar moment to when AJAX came out and then everyone's just like, "Wow, you can build new things here." So it feels like there's a lesson here of just, "If there's a new technology that has enabled, something big that we think may, let's just work there for a while, and see if something comes up." (00:25:35): And then I think the other lesson here is just, as a founder, just survive as long as you can. Because you may find something that works.
turns.zh:
这一历程中有很多非常有趣的经验教训，其中一些甚至与常规思维背道而驰。比如，你最初是先开发技术，再去寻找需要解决的问题。这恰恰是人们常告诫你不要采取的做法，但这次却成功了。（00:25:19）  
另一个有趣的启示是，这感觉就像AJAX刚问世时的情景，当时所有人都惊呼：“哇，这里能开发出新东西！” 所以这里有一个经验：当新技术带来重大机遇时，我们不妨先埋头开发，观察是否能催生出创新应用。（00:25:35）  
另外，我认为作为创始人，最重要的是尽可能延续生存期。因为说不定你就能找到成功的突破口。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: All great points, all great points. Because you're dead right. And fortunately, my co-founder and I had, we had built a lot of unsuccessful stars before this. We spend most of the, or 20 times, churning through ideas on things. So when we had conviction, I was like, "This seems like a technology that will be important." It seems like, the web is the most ubiquitous... The pitch or the theory in our head was like, "The web is the most ubiquitous platform in the world, but yet it has no, you can't use the web to build the web." (00:26:08): Every other platform, Mac has Xcode. Windows has Visual Studio. The web had nothing. And we were like, "At a minimum, Google should probably buy this thing from us. It seems like it should probably be part of Chrome," at a minimum. And we thought, "Hey, this could be a huge enabler." The vision of just making it as easy to build full stack applications as using Canva, it just seemed really compelling. (00:26:43): But when you do that sort of risky deep technology play, you need to... And we were very good about this, like the previous company Albert and I did, we bootstrapped it all the way through to acquisition, so we understood and we were living hand-to-mouth, to bootstrap that thing. So we understood out of it how to have a low burn rate, and take a lot of shots on goal, and make every dollar stretch beyond what anyone would think is reasonable or possible. And that's how we played our hands with StackBlitz. We didn't raise money for the first two or three years of the company's life. We were bootstrapping it. When we did raise money, we barely spent it. Largely because it was like, "We need to just take a lot of smart bets, and it doesn't make sense." (00:27:32): And I would just say generally, until you see pull, just people pulling the product out of your hands, you don't want to be spending money. You should be like, default, no. And when you go and buy software, you should be going, "We're a tiny startup. Can you sell it for half?" Everything you buy, just keep the burn rate as low as possible, because you need as many shots on goal as you can possibly get. Because you have no idea. I think just generally, for startups, that's the right way in my view, to approach it. Unless you're seeing, again, immediate demand and pull, or whatever. (00:28:02): But yeah, I think that'd be, maybe the extra context I'd add on top is, I think that we ended up doing a good job of being extremely conservative. During a time in which, during 2020, through 2020 and 2021, which were times where exuberance and growing headcount was like, KPIs of companies. And were things that were being... With lot of emotional force of like, "Hey, you guys ought to be doing this." And I'm glad that we didn't heed the advice, because if we had tripled the company and kicked up the burn rate, there would be no Bolt. We would've gone out of business a lot of time ago. (00:28:48): So I think that's the hard thing about being an entrepreneur, I think is you kind of have to... There are periods of time where you have to make judgment calls that are not going to be the consensus view. Maybe years later, it'll become the consensus view, but you got to have confidence in your convictions on how to best play the hand.
turns.zh: 全都是好点子！全都是好点子！因为你说得太对了。幸运的是，我和联合创始人此前曾打造过许多失败的项目。我们花了大量时间（大约20次）反复构思各种想法。直到我们坚定信念时，我才意识到：“这项技术必将举足轻重。” 网络平台本应是普及至极的……但当时我们的理念是：“网络是全球最普及的平台，却无法用其构建网络本身的应用。” （00:26:08）其他平台如Mac有Xcode，Windows有Visual Studio，唯独网络一无所有。我们当时想：“谷歌至少应该从我们这里收购这项技术。它本该成为Chrome的一部分。” （00:26:43）但当你涉足高风险的深度技术领域时，必须……我们在这方面做得很出色。比如我和Albert创立的Albert公司，我们全程自力更生直至被收购，因此深知如何在最低成本下运营。（00:27:32）在公司成立的头两三年，我们从不融资，全凭自力更生。即便后来融资，也极少动用资金，主要因为我们坚信：“必须抓住大量明智的机遇，合理利用每一分钱。” （00:28:02）总之，在用户真正抢购产品之前，切莫轻易烧钱。应保持默认策略：拒绝融资。购买软件时，要砍价至半价。一切开支都要尽可能压低成本，因为你根本无法预测未来。对我而言，初创企业就该以这种谨慎策略为核心，除非能立即看到需求与反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many great lessons here, I think just this idea of just staying alive. Dalton came on the podcast, he's a partner at YC Ones, and he just had this phrase, "Just don't die." And that's exactly what you guys did, seven years of just trying it until something worked, and I love that you actually were planning to shut down the company right before you launched Bolt. And I know you launched it with just a tweet, right? That was the launch moment?
turns.zh: 里面有很多宝贵的经验，我觉得最重要的就是要坚持下去。达尔顿做客播客时，他是YC Ones的合伙人，当时他说了一句话：“只要别死掉。”而你们正是这么做的，七年里不断尝试，直到找到成功的路径。我很欣赏你们在推出Bolt前还打算关闭公司的决心。我记得你们当时只是发了一条推文就上线了吧？那就是正式发布的时刻吧？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yep. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe talk about that moment of just, after launch, signs that, "Okay, this is working. Something's different."
turns.zh: 能否谈谈上线后那些表明“嗯，产品确实成功了，有些地方变了”的时刻？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. So day one it was like, there's great reception to the tweet. We were like, "Wow, this is one of the biggest things, launch day reception we've ever seen." And I think on the first day, I think we added 60K of ARR, or something. Which was like, I mean, crazy. Again, we were at 600, so we added 10% in a day. And I remember our dev ops engineer, he was the one who would flag me. He was like, "Guys, we got 60K today. This is crazy." And I was like, "Yeah, yeah. But this is launch day." (00:30:12): There's the tech crunch, peak of initiation, in the classic startup-
turns.zh: 对，对。第一天推文反响热烈。我们当时就惊叹：“哇，这是我们见过最成功的上线日反馈了。” 我记得第一天新增了6万美元的ARR（年度经常性收入），简直太疯狂了。我们之前只有600美元，所以一天就增长了10%。我记得我们的运维工程师提醒我：“伙计们，今天新增了6万美元，太不可思议了。” 我当时就说：“是啊是啊，但这可是上线日啊。”（00:30:12）：经典的创业公司阶段——技术瓶颈、初创高峰期——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [Inaudible 00:30:17]-

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: ... star, yeah. I was like, "Listen, guys." I'm trying to temper enthusiasm for the team. I'm like, "This is great. Got a lot of work to do." And then the next day we added 80K, or whatever it was, and it just kind of kept going. And all the while, the product we put out, we built a thing in 90 days. We built Bolt in 90. So there's a lot of things that were missing in the product. Like, basic stuff, basic stuff. And which, again, we cut the right corners on the thing to get it online, but we had this just growing influx of people using it, going, "How is there not a mobile responsive view? How are chat messages not," we got to 20 million of ARR without a mobile responsive view, by the way. Just throwing that out there. It was like the iPhone not having copy and paste until iPhone 5, or whatever. That was that, this was that for us, it was like, no mobile. You looked at it on mobile, it was terrible. (00:31:13): But there was stuff like that, so we had to just... And then, we're a small team and so, we were completely unprepared for just the growing traffic. And there was a whole bunch, I mean, the list of problems that were happening every single day was nuts. I mean, to start, we had never had a plan on stackblitz.com for more than $9.00. We had one price, nine bucks. And so when we launched Bolt we were like, "Again, we don't think, hopefully people like this, but nine bucks doesn't get you a lot of inference." And so people burn through nine bucks in 48 hours. And they're like, "I want to buy more. How do I buy more? Why won't you take my money?" (00:31:56): So it was like, within the week we rolled out just completely new pricing plans, where you could upgrade, which ended up, has kind of now become the standard. All the other guys in the space have copied this. Where prior to Bolt going online, Copilot, all these previous AI things, everyone wanted this Netflix model where there's one price, it's like all you can eat, or whatever. And the problem is, if you do that, you want the inference cost to be kind of low, because you're expecting people to use it a lot. And so you can't do these agentic experience things, it would be too expensive. (00:32:29): And what we ended up stumbling into is that, "Okay, actually, people are willing to pay more. People want to pay for more inference, because we've crossed this threshold where you can get a very tangible ROI." You know that this is providing a tremendous amount of value to you. So anyways, that was one thing, and the servers were just melting. Anthropic ran out of GPUs for us. Dario emailed me, he was like, "Listen, we don't have anything more to give you." At the times, where we're like, "How do we deal with..." It was just bananas, for weeks. It felt like in 300, when they're surrounded by 10,000 people, and our team is just doing everything. There's 15, 20 people, just doing everything. My chief of staff and I were doing customer support 95% of the day. Anyways. (00:33:22): So yeah, it was a crazy wild time. I mean, it still is. We've had a little bit more time to grow into this. And usually, I mean as a company, to grow into even 20 million ARR, you get a year at least or something, to kind of staff up.
turns.zh: ……明星，对吧？我当时就说：“听着，伙计们。”我试图给团队降降温。我说：“这很棒，但还有很多工作要做。” 结果第二天我们就新增了8万用户，或者其他什么数字，然后用户量就一直涨个不停。与此同时，我们推出的产品，90天内就做出来了。但产品里有很多缺失的功能，比如最基本的功能。再说了，为了让产品上线，我们在某些地方偷了懒，但用户量还是不断增长，他们纷纷抱怨：“为什么没有移动端响应式界面？为什么聊天消息没有……” 顺便说一句，我们在没有移动端响应式界面的情况下，就达到了2000万的年营收目标。就像iPhone 5之前没有复制粘贴功能一样。这对我们来说就是挑战，没有移动端体验，用户体验太差了。（00:31:13）但还有其他问题，我们完全没准备好应对日益增长的流量。每天出现的问题多得离谱。比如，StackBlitz.com从来没有超过9美元的定价。我们只有9美元一个价位。当我们推出Bolt时，我们想：“希望人们喜欢它，但9美元买不到太多算力。”结果用户在48小时内就把9美元花光了。他们问：“我想多买点怎么买？为什么不收钱？” （00:31:56）于是我们在一周内推出了全新的定价方案，用户可以升级订阅，这套模式现在成了行业标准。Bolt上线前，Copilot和其他AI产品都想复制Netflix那种一价制的模式，但问题是，如果你想让用户大量使用，就得把算力成本压低，这样才能不增加成本。但那样就没法提供智能交互体验了。（00:32:29）最后我们发现，用户愿意为更高的算力付费，因为他们看到了实实在在的ROI。总之，这是一次摸索的过程。服务器崩溃了，Anthropic给我们的GPU用完了。达里奥发邮件说：“我们没法给你更多资源了。” 当时我们焦头烂额，整整几周都忙得像疯人。就像《300》里被1万人围攻，而我们团队只有15-20人拼命应战。我的幕僚长和我每天95%的时间都在做客服。总之，（00:33:22）那真是疯狂的时期。到现在还是。好在我们有更多时间调整。通常来说，公司要达到2000万年营收目标，至少需要一年的时间来扩充团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Often, decades.
turns.zh: 通常是几十年。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah. So that was as hard, we'd go to people and kind of be like, "What do we do?" And the playbooks we get back are, take six months, or a year, or something. It's like, "This isn't going to work." Which is funny, this is what it's all about. I mean this is, at least for me, that level of intensity, it's challenging. Fun challenges, you know?
turns.zh: 是啊。这真的很艰难。我们去找别人，然后就问：“我们该怎么办？”而对方给出的解决方案往往是，等六个月、一年之类的。但我们心里想：“这根本行不通啊。”说起来挺有趣的，但这正是关键所在。至少对我来说，这种高强度的挑战很有挑战性。但也是很有趣的挑战，你懂吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, okay. This is just nonstop wild, wild shit. So you mentioned that your team was about 20 people through all of this, you guys are growing at this insane rate, 20 people. How was this possible? What has allowed you to grow this much, this fast, with such a small team? And this 300 visual is interesting, I imagine having these Spartans is a big part of it. Just what has allowed you to do this?
turns.zh: 哇，好。真是太疯狂、太不可思议了。你之前提到整个过程中你的团队大概有20个人，你们以如此惊人的速度在增长，20个人？这怎么可能呢？是什么让你们能在如此小的团队规模下实现如此快速的增长？还有这个300的视觉效果很有趣，我想这些“斯巴达战士”（指高效的团队成员）一定是关键因素。到底是什么让你们能做到这些？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah, I think a lot of it again, I mean if you kind of look at where a lot of the other folks, like the Cogen types of app space, have really been struggling, a lot of it has been scaling their servers with stuff. And it was kind of like both this overnight success, seven years in the making. All of this stuff, there's no way, if you rewind to year two, there's no way we could have, we would not be at the growth on DAUs, and revenue, or whatever. There's just no way. And so a lot of it is the technology we made, and most importantly, it's been the people. (00:35:19): The people... It's rare to find startups where you have the core group of five, six, seven people, that have been there for five years, plus. That's a pretty rare thing to see in Silicon Valley. It is usually, folks are at a startup for a year or two, they kind of go to another one. You know what I mean? And the problem with the turnover like that is that you can't take really long bets like the one we did. And so we've had, kind of from the get-go, again, this comes back from bootstrapping the previous company. Just having less people, and more context per head. That's just been how we do it, and we feel very strongly about it. (00:36:00): And the reason for that is, one, that you can have high levels of trust with anyone you're talking to, because you know that they have a lot of context. It's not like this person's completely in the dark, in some corner of the company that doesn't... You know what I mean? The second thing, everyone has agency to actually get stuff done, front to back. And there's no political community to get stuff approved by, there's no... So when you look at what happened with Bolt, I mean, we had engineers that were, front to back, were on a call with someone running into an issue, going and fixing it. Cooking up the UI on the spot, and landing this thing. Without involving anyone else on the team. (00:36:41): So I think it was the culmination of just high trust, and people, we all just have enjoyed working together in the past. Maybe that's why, that's the only reason that anyone would ever stay at a company for that long, or whatever. And so those sorts of stressful situations, I think, are make or break. Those are make or break for any team. And so, I think that what's happened is really, it is a direct reflection of the strength and the bonds of the people that are making this thing, and supporting the thing.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得关键在于，如果你看看其他很多公司，比如Cogen这类应用领域的公司，他们在扩展服务器方面遇到了很多困难。而我们这种overnight success（一夜成名）的案例，背后却花了七年的时间打磨。所有这些成就，要是回溯到第二年，根本不可能达成我们现在在DAU（每日活跃用户）和营收等方面的增长目标。根本不可能。所以很大程度上要归功于我们开发的技术，但最重要的是团队的人才。（00:35:19）：团队成员……很难找到那种核心团队由五、六、七个人组成，并且能坚持五年以上的人。这种情况在硅谷实属罕见。通常人们在一家初创公司待一两年后，就会跳槽到其他公司。你懂我的意思吧？人员流动率高会导致你无法像我们这样进行长期的战略布局。所以从一开始，我们就沿用了之前初创公司的模式——团队规模小，成员之间沟通顺畅。这就是我们的工作方式，也是我们坚信不移的理念。（00:36:00）：原因有两个：首先，与任何人沟通时都能建立高度信任，因为他们对项目有充分的了解，不存在信息不对称的情况。不会有那种人在公司某个角落里蒙头干活的情况，你懂我的意思吧？其次，团队成员从头到尾都有自主决策权，无需层层审批。例如，Bolt项目中，工程师们能直接参与到问题的解决过程中，当场设计UI并完成任务，无需其他团队成员参与。（00:36:41）：所以我认为这正是高信任度和团队协作的结晶。我们过去一直很享受一起工作的时光。也许这就是人们愿意长期留在一家公司的唯一原因。在面对高压情况时，团队的凝聚力至关重要。正是因为团队成员的强大和紧密合作，才成就了今天的成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's such an important point, that you guys have been working together for many years. Most people won't have that benefit. When you're hiring people, when you hire this initial team, is there anything you look for that you think maybe people aren't looking for enough? Anything you prioritize when you're hiring new folks? Is it this idea that they can do a lot? They can do customer calls, they can do design, they can do engineering?
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这是一个很重要的一点——你们团队已经合作多年了。大多数人可没有这样的优势。在招聘团队时，尤其是初创团队，您有没有特别看重但人们可能不太重视的方面？在招聘新人时，您会优先考虑哪些因素？比如，他们是否能胜任多项工作？比如客户沟通、设计、工程开发等？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah, for us, and even if the folks were hiring us, hiring people that don't care about the titles, and they don't care about... It's not like they're... People, of course it's people have a career trajectory, and that sort of thing, but they really are motivated by just working on cool things, and are chucking their ego at the door. And they're there to collectively build something great, not just kind of follow, and be the brilliant jerk. Most of the people that we've hired have been in Europe. We're a fully remote company. My co-founder and I are in the Bay Area. It's funny, back in 2018, we rented an office and stuff, and we were commuting into it. Because we thought we'd hire people here, and like a year into it we were like, "What are we doing? You and I are coming to an office for 10 people, we've hired, the people working for us are in Europe, or across the US." And we have one or two other people we've hired that are in the Bay Area at this point. (00:38:51): But yeah, I think we kind of look for folks that are intrinsically just trying to build great stuff, and are interested. And then the first people that we hired, the reason that we found them is that they were users of StackBlitz. A lot of people, the majority of people we've hired at the company have been people that actually came from our community, basically. So when we want to hire people, we put out a tweet and say, "Hey, we're hiring an engineer," and then we get DMs or whatever. (00:39:22): But yeah, those are the general kind of qualities we look for, though.
turns.zh: 是的，对我们来说，即便别人来招聘我们，也会优先选择那些不在乎头衔、不在乎……我说他们不是不在乎……当然，人都有职业发展路径之类的，但他们真正被驱动的，就是想做酷炫的事情，并且愿意放下自负。他们来是为了共同创造伟大的事业，而不是只想做个自以为是的混蛋。我们招聘的大多数人都在欧洲。我们是一家完全远程办公的公司。我和我的联合创始人在湾区。说起来挺有趣的，2018年我们租了办公室之类的，还每天通勤去上班。因为我们当时以为会在湾区招人，结果一年后，我们意识到：“我们在做什么？你和我每天跑去为10个人服务的办公室，而我们招来的员工都在欧洲或者全美各地。”现在湾区只有一两个新员工。（00:38:51）不过，我觉得我们更看重那些本质上就想创造伟大事物、充满热情的人。我们最初招聘的那些人，都是因为他们是StackBlitz的用户才被我们发现的。我们公司的大多数新员工，基本上都是从我们的社区中招来的。所以当我们想招聘时，就会发推文说：“嘿，我们要招聘工程师”，然后就会收到私信之类的。（00:39:22）不过，这些确实是我们普遍看重的品质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to chat with Christina Gilbert, the founder of OneSchema, one of our long-time podcast sponsors. Hi, Christina.
turns.zh: 我很高兴能与OneSchema的创始人克里斯蒂娜·吉尔伯特交流，她是我们播客的长期赞助商之一。嗨，克里斯蒂娜。

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Yes. Thank you for having me on, Lenny.
turns.zh: 是的。感谢邀请我参加节目，伦尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the latest with OneSchema? I know you now work with some of my favorite companies like Ramp, Vanta, Scale and Watershed. I heard that you just launched a new product to help product teams import CSVs from especially tricky systems like ERPs?
turns.zh: OneSchema最近有什么新动态吗？我知道你现在与Ramp、Vanta、Scale和Watershed等我最喜欢的公司合作。我听说你们刚推出了一个新产品，帮助产品团队从ERP等复杂系统导入CSV文件？

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Yes, so we just launched OneSchema FileFeeds, which allows you to build an integration with any system in 15 minutes, as long as you can export a CSV to an SFTP folder. We see our customers all the time getting stuck with hacks, and workarounds, and the product teams that we work with don't have to turn down prospects because their systems are too hard to integrate with. We allow our customers to offer thousands of integrations without involving their engineering team at all.
turns.zh: 是的，我们刚推出了OneSchema FileFeeds，它能让你在15分钟内与任何系统建立集成，只要该系统能将CSV文件导出到SFTP文件夹即可。我们经常看到客户被各种临时解决方案困住，而与我们合作的产品团队再也不用因为系统集成太难而拒绝潜在客户了。我们让客户无需动用工程团队，就能提供数千种集成服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can tell you that if my team had to build integrations like this, how nice would it be to be able to take this off my roadmap, and instead use something like OneSchema. And not just to build it, but also to maintain it forever.
turns.zh: 我可以告诉你，如果我的团队要开发这样的集成功能，能把这部分从路线图中移除，转而使用OneSchema这样的工具，那该有多好啊。这不仅能节省开发时间，还能实现永久维护。

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Absolutely, Lenny. We've heard so many horror stories of multi-day outages, from even just a handful of bad records. We are laser focused on integration reliability to help teams end all of those distractions that come up with integrations. We have a built-in validation layer that stops any bad data from entering your system, and OneSchema will notify your team immediately of any data that looks incorrect.
turns.zh: 没错，莱尼。我们听过太多因少数不良记录导致多日系统瘫痪的可怕故事。我们正全力确保集成的可靠性，帮助团队消除集成过程中出现的各种干扰。我们内置的验证层能阻止错误数据进入系统，一旦发现数据异常，OneSchema会立即通知团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that importing incorrect data can cause all kinds of pain for your customers, and quickly lose their trust. Christina, thank you for joining us, and if you want to learn more head on over to oneschema.co, that's oneschema.co. (00:41:01): I want to ask a couple more questions about Bolt, and then I want to zoom out, and talk about where things are heading in the future. Let's talk about prioritization. I imagine you guys are just barraged with, as you described, after you launched, you're just barraged with requests. Like you said, there's a million monthly active users. I can't even imagine the feature requests you guys are getting, plus all the stuff you know want to build. Just how do you go about deciding what to prioritize, and what to actually build?
turns.zh: 我知道导入错误数据会让客户深感困扰，并迅速失去他们的信任。克里斯蒂娜，感谢你的加入。如果你想了解更多信息，请访问oneschema.co（00:41:01）。我想再问几个关于Bolt的问题，然后再放宽视野，谈谈未来发展方向。首先谈谈优先级管理。我想你们团队在产品上线后，就像你描述的那样，被各种请求淹没。毕竟每月有百万活跃用户，我简直无法想象你们收到的功能请求数量，再加上你们自己想开发的功能。你们是如何确定优先级、决定实际开发哪些功能的？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: There's a lot of things that you just don't even know are possible to do, and so, people aren't going to be necessarily explicitly asking for them. And so there's been kind of a couple of these, where we use our gut instinct on like, "Hey, no one's asking for this, in meaningful numbers at least. But we think this is going to be a big deal." (00:41:47): Best example was last week with native mobile app support. That's, by reception, the biggest thing we've ever launched. And it was something that, even internally at the company, some folks were like, "This, I don't know. People are yelling about these other things." And it is, it's always this balance of how much are we just triaging various things, versus that new capabilities, but it was like, "This strikes me as an important one," where we put some chips into the middle of the table on. And had it dead right. It's just this mind-blowing experience, and now, there's just thousands of mobile apps being created a day, that weren't before. And how does that change things? I mean, now there's small businesses that, they would've never made an iPhone app before. It made no sense. It's super expensive. Now, that's not the case. (00:42:43): So there's kind of these things where it's like, "Hey, we should go and take bets here." But there's kind of this, I think the best analogy would be like, it's kind of like working at a restaurant, being like a chef. There's some amount of, there's feedback from the customers of, "This thing didn't taste good." And then there's like, "Hey, we've been cooking something interesting, and this tastes... I don't know. This, I think you're going to like this. I think this is a killer dish." And so you kind of have to balance those things. (00:43:15): And I think it's actually, largely, a function of just years of experience doing it. I think if you kind of rewound 10 years ago, I would have had really no, I wouldn't have had just the years of getting my butt kicked by the free market, to have cultivated a sense of this stuff. You kind of have to build your own gun and stick for it, I guess is the best way of putting it.
turns.zh:
有很多功能其实人们根本不知道存在的可能性，所以用户未必会明确提出需求。比如我们就曾根据直觉判断，"虽然目前没有太多用户要求，但我们认为这个功能会带来重大价值"。（00:41:47）上周推出的原生移动应用支持就是最佳例子。从反馈来看，这是我们推出的最受欢迎功能。甚至公司内部有些人还在质疑："这东西谁需要啊？大家都在关注其他功能。" 但事实证明，我们押对了宝。这带来了令人惊叹的体验，现在每天都有数千个移动应用被开发出来，而此前根本没有这个市场。这种变化对小企业影响巨大——他们以前根本不会考虑开发iPhone应用，这根本不划算，现在却能轻松实现。
（00:42:43）有些决策就像在餐厅当厨师。顾客反馈"这道菜不好吃"，但厨师可能坚持说："这道菜很特别，味道...我觉得你们会喜欢的。"这就需要平衡各方意见。（00:43:15）这其实源于多年的经验积累。若回到10年前，我根本没有机会在自由市场中历经挫折，从而培养出这种敏锐的判断力。可以说，成功的秘诀就是不断磨练自己的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To unpack this a little bit further, do you have a cadence you guys work through to decide what to build, and ship? Do you have a weekly meeting every week? Because I know the answer is probably, really, "It's just chaos constantly, and fires we're putting out constantly." I know that's a lot of it, but is there some kind of process that you guys have for deciding what to build, and how to share it, and just work with the team?
turns.zh: 稍微深入探讨一下，你们有没有一个固定的工作流程来决定要开发和发布什么产品？每周都有例会吗？因为我知道答案很可能是，"这完全就是一团乱麻，我们每天都在救火。"我知道这确实是现实情况，但你们是否有某种流程来决定要开发什么产品、如何分享信息以及与团队协作？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: We all meet every day. Pretty much the entire team gets on a call, and we just kind of front to back-
turns.zh: 我们每天都会开会。基本上整个团队都会参加电话会议，从头到尾讨论所有事情——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You meet, like a Zoom?
turns.zh: 你们用的是Zoom吗？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah, every day at 8:00 AM Pacific, we're on a Zoom for at least an hour-
turns.zh: 是的，太平洋时间每天早上8点，我们都会用Zoom开会至少一个小时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Every day? The whole company?
turns.zh: 每天全公司都参加吗？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Pretty much the entire company. Yeah.
turns.zh: 基本上全公司都会参加。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. For an hour. Okay.
turns.zh: 哇。一个小时啊。好的。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah. And we just go over everything and I think we're going to probably start, as the team's kind of growing, we're going to start splintering off into different syncs, or whatever. But the thing about just having everyone in the same room every day is that, a lot of people will complain that it's... On Twitter, you'll see people say, "Oh, it's the most expensive use of everyone's time," but it's like, "Yep. But there's 0% fidelity loss in that. Everything, every day, is being audited front to back, and being discussed front to back." (00:44:47): So when you're in these times of just extreme growth, you want as close to 0% loss, on communications. And so that's how we've been doing it, especially since Bolt went online, and I think it was the week after Bolt went online we were like, "Every day, until we're through this or whatever, we're all getting on a phone call every day, and we're front to back doing this." And again, another reason why more context and less heads, every person at the company is aware of everything else going on at the company. So people can independently be making decisions that are generally, by default, more often correct than not.
turns.zh: 是的。随着团队规模扩大，我们可能会分成不同的组别。但每天让所有人都在同一房间开会的好处是，很多人会抱怨这太耗时间了。在推特上，你会看到人们说：“这简直是浪费大家时间的最昂贵方式。”但其实，信息传递的准确性是100%的。每天的每件事都会被前后审计、反复讨论。（00:44:47）所以在快速增长的时期，你希望沟通环节的信息准确性接近0%。所以这就是我们一直采取的做法，特别是自从Bolt上线以来，那周我们就决定：“在完成当前任务之前，我们每天都要开会，从头到尾讨论所有事情。” 再说一次，这也是为什么公司需要更少的层级和更多上下沟通的原因。公司里的每个人都能了解其他部门的动态。因此，人们可以独立做出决策，而这些决策通常默认是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting. I've never heard that before. Especially for company growing, that is like yours. That is super interesting, that that's what you do.
turns.zh: 这太有趣了。我以前从未听说过这种做法。特别是对于像你们这样快速发展的公司来说，这真的很有意思。你们这样做真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: I don't think we're going to do that forever.
turns.zh: 我不认为我们会永远这样做下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Of course.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: But, yeah.
turns.zh: 不过，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, but I think that's a really cool thing to note, that that works. And has worked for you. Where do you, so say you talk about stuff, then where do you put stuff? Where do you put your roadmap? Where do you plan? Just, what tools are kind of in the stack of the company's toolset?
turns.zh: 不，但我认为这是一个值得注意的成功案例，它确实有效，对你们也很有效。那么，你们是如何讨论这些事情的，然后又把这些信息存储在哪里呢？你们的路线图放在哪里？你们如何规划？公司的工具堆里都有哪些工具呢？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah, on the engineering side, we use Linear heavily. On kind of product roadmapping, we're using Notion, and kind of making PRD type stuff in Notion. And we use Figma for design. No, actually, we use Bolt for a lot of design and prototyping at this point, as you can imagine. But yeah, I think that the tooling is nothing crazy. There's nothing crazy sophisticated. I think we'll be investing a lot more, and especially as you start splintering people out of being on the same call every day, so that's where this stuff really starts to matter. Because you don't have a time where you're able to dynamically catch things that weren't going to be brought up.
turns.zh: 是的，在工程方面，咱们大量使用了 Linear。在产品路线规划方面，我们使用 Notion，在 Notion 中制作类似 PRD（产品需求文档）的东西。设计方面则用 Figma。不过说实话，目前我们更多地使用 Bolt 进行设计和原型制作，这大家应该能想象得到。但我觉得这些工具并没有什么特别复杂的地方。未来我们会投入更多精力，尤其是当团队成员不再需要每天开会时，此时这些工具就显得尤为重要了。因为那样就没有机会及时发现未被提及的问题了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you guys use PRDs. I love that you even used that term. There's a lot of talk of just like, "Oh, we got Bolt now we got all these tools, we don't need PRDs. We're just going to create a prototype immediately, and that's it." Talk about just why you still find that useful, and just what you put into your PRD, whatever that is for you.
turns.zh: 我很高兴你们还在用 PRD。我喜欢你们用这个术语。现在有很多讨论，比如“哦，我们用了 Bolt，现在有了一堆工具，就不需要 PRD了。我们直接做原型就行。”但我想问问你们，为什么仍然觉得 PRD 有用？你们在 PRD 里都写些什么？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Unless there's something that's very sophisticated that we're working on, we tend to keep them pretty light. I like to just have the minimal amount of context possible, that just ensures everyone's on the same page and that the key outcomes for whatever feature that we're working on, are going to be present when we get there. Because the things that, when these arguments get really beefy, you're looking at it at, "God, there's so much stuff to decipher." The problem is, a lot of people are going to gloss over it when it gets kicked to development, or design, or whatever. It's just going to start snowballing into a lot of stuff. It's just better to keep it as simple as you possibly can. At least, that's our approach to the thing. And often it's some of these things are like, "Here's a link to a Bolt."
turns.zh: 除非我们在处理非常复杂的项目，否则 PRD 通常都很简洁。我喜欢把上下文控制在最低限度，确保每个人都清楚重点。当我们开发某个功能时，关键成果都能一目了然。这很重要，因为当争论变得激烈时，大家会发现有太多内容需要解析。但很多时候，这些内容在交给开发或设计团队后，就会被忽略掉，最终变成一堆问题。简洁明了最好。至少这是我们的做法。通常 PRD 里会附上 Bolt 的链接。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: "And here's what it might look like."
turns.zh: “这大概就是最终效果的样子。”

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah. And not just look like, "Here's kind of a working demo of what it will effectively feel like." And then, be. Because that just, if a picture is worth a thousand words, a live actual demo is worth millions. You can feel it. It's real. And that's what we're seeing, a lot of the businesses that are adopting Bolt now, that's the use case that they're using this for. Is high fidelity prototyping, because it's now faster to make real prototypes using Bolt. Before, it was too expensive. The idea of, "And let's prototype it, the engineers' code a proto..." It's like, that, it would take forever. It would be expensive. And now it's faster to do this with Bolt, in code, and have a real working software product, than dragging around frames and Figma to actually make a static version of it.
turns.zh: 是的。不只是展示效果，“这大概就是实际的演示效果。”然后再实际操作。因为一张图片胜过千言万语，一个实用的演示胜过千张图片。你能真切感受到它是真实的。我们观察到，现在很多采用 Bolt 的公司都在用它来做高保真原型设计，因为现在用 Bolt 做原型更快了。以前成本太高了。那种“先做个原型，再让工程师写代码实现原型”的做法，太耗时耗钱了。现在用 Bolt 用代码就能快速做出可用的软件产品，比用 Figma 制作静态版本要高效得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's actually talk about that. Just how far have companies gotten with Bolt? Prototypes is where everyone's kind of imagining these tools are at. I know that the goal isn't just to make prototypes, it's to build full scale. I imagine, long-term, Salesforce, Atlassian style companies, at scale. What are some examples of products people have built with Bolt that maybe would surprise people, in just how far they've gotten?
turns.zh: 那咱们来聊聊这个。企业用 Bolt 到底达到了什么程度？原型设计是大家想象中这些工具的应用场景。我知道目标不只是做原型，而是要打造完整的产品。我能想象，长期来看，像 Salesforce、Atlassian 这样的公司会大规模应用 Bolt。有什么用 Bolt 开发的产品案例能让人惊讶于他们的进展？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, especially... When you're starting greenfield stuff, you can use Bolt to build... you know. Like Salesforce, as an example. One of the first people that signed up for Bolt was this guy named Paul, and he's an entrepreneur, and doesn't know how to code. Built a CRM in three weeks, that has AI built into it and Stripe for billing, et cetera. He had gotten a quote from an agency for this, it was going to be 30 grand, and take six months. He had done in three weeks, and I think he spent 300 bucks on Bolt for the thing. So it's like, this is... And he's making money off of this. This is his start. Right?
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说，特别是……当你从零开始开发新项目时，你可以用Bolt来搭建……你懂的。比如Salesforce就是个例子。最早注册Bolt的用户之一叫保罗，他是个创业者，但完全不会编程。他在三周内就搭建了一个CRM系统，里面集成了AI功能，还接入了Stripe支付等服务。他原本找代理机构报价要3万美元，花六个月时间才能完成。而他用Bolt只花了300美元。简直难以置信，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so he built this, and he's selling it. People are paying to use it.
turns.zh: 好的，他开发了这个产品，现在还在出售，用户愿意付费使用。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: And there's many such cases of this. If you're looking at greenfield projects, 100%. Today with this current state of frontier models, you could absolutely build production grade software. You're not going to get a zero shot, but you're going to spend a couple of days, weeks, whatever. But the cost reduction there, 30 grand versus $300. It's 99% cheaper. Six months versus three weeks. I mean, it's like order of magnitude sort of fashioned delivery on the thing. And those numbers have helped, for the people that we talk to, that are building these full stack apps. People, they go to Upwork, work, they get a quote for five grand. They have it within 50 bucks. It's just nuts, what you're able to do with this thing. (00:50:35): And so I think on the flip side, a lot of the existing companies, there are very legitimate use cases where things are greenfield, spun up. A good example is public websites. Marketing pages, landing pages, whatever have you. Folks are adopting Bolt to just power those instead of using Webflow, for example. Because it's like, this is simpler to use than Webflow. And it integrates with the existing design system of the company, and et cetera. And the marketers can update it without knowing how to code, whatever. But then for product development teams, this is most commonly for, again, existing software businesses. They're using this to just accelerate the product development process, and in a way where it's not just like a Greenfield wholesale, "Hey, we're building the entire thing in Bolt," or whatever.
turns.zh:
这样的案例还有很多。如果你着眼于全新项目，100%能做到。以当前的前沿模式为例，你绝对能开发出生产级别的软件。虽然不保证成功，但只要花几天或几周时间就能完成。但成本差别巨大，3万美元对比300美元，差了99%。六个月对比三周，简直是天壤之别。这些数字对我们接触的那些开发全栈应用的人很有帮助。人们去Upwork找人开发，报价要5千美元，而用Bolt只需50美元。简直不可思议，用这个工具能做这么多事。
（00:50:35）：另外，从另一方面看，很多现有公司也有合理的用例，比如全新搭建的项目。典型的例子就是公共网站、营销页面、着陆页之类的。人们用Bolt来替代Webflow，因为Bolt比Webflow更易用，还能与现有设计系统集成，营销人员无需懂编程就能更新内容。不过对于产品开发团队来说，最常见的应用场景还是现有软件公司。他们用Bolt来加速产品开发过程，而不是一股脑地全盘托管整个项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can Bolt integrate with your existing code base, or not yet?
turns.zh: Bolt能否与现有代码库集成，还是暂时不行？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: So yeah, we can actually open up repos in Bolt. You can go and use Bolt on your code base. It kind of depends on your setup. And we do have companies, again, that have marketing sites they're using this on, or their admin panel or whatever. And I think it's going to be a use case that we see a lot more people orienting towards. These LLMs are not great, depending on how big your application is, though. These things are not quite there, where if you have something that's a thousand files or something, or more, where you're going to be able to have a really reliable, super reliable experience per se. Within a year, we'll chat a year from now, I suspect the answer is going to be different. So it kind of depends on the size of the app, the scale of the app, and if it's too big, you're looking at the prototyping, just pure acceleration of product development. And if it's not, then you can just do it entirely from Bolt.
turns.zh: 是的，我们确实可以在Bolt中开设代码仓库。你可以把Bolt应用到现有代码库上，但这取决于你的具体配置。我们确实有一些公司，比如用Bolt开发营销网站、管理面板之类的。我觉得这种用例会越来越普及。不过这些大语言模型（LLMs）目前还不太靠谱，取决于你的应用规模有多大。对于千行级别的代码库，LLMs目前还无法提供真正可靠的体验。不过一年后再聊，我相信答案会不一样。所以这取决于应用的规模和复杂度，如果规模太大，可能只能用于原型设计，加速产品开发；如果规模适中，完全可以全程用Bolt开发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this is useful. So what would you say are the major limitations of Bolt today, where people should just know, "Okay, it's not going to get you here yet. Maybe in the future it will." So it sounds like, if you have a really large existing code base, probably not the best tool yet. What else should people know?
turns.zh: 嗯，这确实很有用。那么你认为Bolt目前主要有哪些局限性呢？人们应该清楚，“好吧，它现在还达不到你的需求，但未来或许会做到。”听起来如果有现有的大型代码库，Bolt可能还不是最佳工具。还有什么其他需要注意的地方呢？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: I would say that's probably the main one, because I think if you have a large existing code base, you're going to need something like Cursor. And you're going to need to be a developer, meaningfully, to be editing that stuff. I think outside of that, there's a, just like using any other productivity tool, like Photoshop or Figma, or like a DSLR or whatever. There's some level of education, and using the tool, and learning how to use it, that's required to really unlock a lot of the maximum capabilities of the thing. (00:53:10): And the people that we see that are most successful with Bolt, outside of developers, the people we see that are most successful are people that are amazing PMs, for example. Because these are people that understand enough about how the technology works, typically, and their job is to direct developers on how to go and improve the product. And go and look into how to actually spec this thing out in a way that's executable, without lossiness in the communication. And when you think about, "Okay, how would you best interact with an AI developer agent?" It's basically that. You really want to be good at defining scope, and helping it go and debug various things, or whatever have you. There's a huge overlap of the skill set of being a rock star PM, and being really good at using, frankly, any of these text to apps or Cogen tools.
turns.zh: 我觉得这可能是最主要的限制，因为如果你有庞大的现有代码库，就需要用到Cursor之类的工具。并且你必须得是开发者，有实际编码经验才能处理这些内容。除此之外，使用任何生产力工具，比如Photoshop、Figma、数码单反相机之类的，都需要一定的学习成本和使用门槛，才能充分发挥其潜力。（00:53:10）：在我们见过的Bolt使用者中，除了开发者外，表现最出色的往往是优秀的产品经理（PM）。因为这些人通常对技术原理有足够的理解，他们的工作是指导开发者如何改进产品，如何以可执行的方式规划产品需求，同时确保沟通无障碍。当你思考“如何与AI开发者代理最有效地合作”时，本质上就是这个道理。你需要善于界定产品范围，帮助他们调试各种问题等等。产品经理（PM）所需的技能与使用文本生成应用或Cogen工具的能力有很大重叠之处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you made that point. That's exactly the point I've been trying to make, I have a newsletter post about this. Because when all these tools came out, there was so many people saying, "Okay, PMs are dead. We don't need them anymore. We can just build things so quickly and easily, what's the point?" But I completely see the world the way you see it. The hard part now is, now it's easy to build the thing. Now it's, "What the hell should we build? Can we clearly articulate what it is we want to build?" And then, "Can we just have the taste to know, is this right, is this correct? Is this good? Is this going to solve the problem?" And then it's like, grow it, which is something also PMs think about. So, I completely agree. Basically it feels like PMs are, and a lot of PMs listen to this, so they'll love hearing this. To me, it feels like PMs are the best positioned role to thrive in this world.
turns.zh: 我很赞同你的观点。这一点正是我一直想强调的，我甚至为此写过一篇通讯文章。当这些工具刚问世时，很多人声称“产品经理已经过时了，我们不再需要他们。我们可以快速轻松地开发产品，还有什么意义呢？” 但我完全认同你的看法。现在的难点在于，开发产品变得容易了。关键问题变成了：“我们到底该开发什么？我们能清晰传达出自己的需求吗？”然后还要有判断力，判断这个想法是否正确、是否有价值、是否能解决问题？接下来就是如何成长，这也是产品经理需要考虑的。所以我完全赞同你的观点。对我来说，产品经理是这个时代最有发展潜力的角色。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Zero question. I mean that was, as Bolt was growing and we were like... Because we were a developer product before this, and so we expected the audience to be 100% developers that were using this. And we just kept seeing more and more and more people that were not developers using it, to the point where it's like, 67% of our users are not developers, at this point. And when I started talking to these folks, at first I was just weird, or whatever. It was like, "Well, what's going on here?" But then it just kind of clicked as like, "Oh, well, this is going to change everything. The entire software world order is going to get rewritten, here." (00:55:30): Because the way that companies are organized to build software today, totally going to change. The idea that again, PMs are the people that really understand, to the pixel level, what matters into making a great product experience. And often they're having... And listen, I'm a developer, myself. They have to go and harangue the developers to get things to be how they really ought to be, to the smallest levels. And now, how this is going to work, if you fast-forward one, two, five years, whatever. PMs, they're going to be "writing code", quote, unquote, instead of just writing a JIRA ticket and waiting for a developer to do it. The developers are going to be able to work on intellectually challenging tasks that LLMs are not well suited for, and still being augmented by LLMs to do it. But PMs are going to be able to go in and just make the changes themselves. (00:56:24): And what blew my mind is, it's not priced in, to any of these companies out there. And it's not reflected in the org charts of all the software companies in the world right now. That is going to completely change. The winners, at least, their org charts are going to completely change, and how they approach building products and shipping products. Completely. And it's starting, this is the beginning.
turns.zh: 毫无疑问。我是说，当Bolt在发展壮大时，我们当时……因为在此之前，我们的产品主要面向开发者，所以我们以为用户群体会100%是使用这款产品的开发者。但后来我们发现越来越多非开发者在使用它，现在我们的用户中67%都不是开发者。当我开始和这些用户交流时，起初我觉得很奇怪，心里想：“这到底是怎么回事？”但后来我突然意识到：“哦，天哪，这一切都将彻底改变。整个软件行业的秩序都将被重写。”（00:55:30）因为如今公司构建软件的组织方式即将彻底变革。再说回产品经理，他们必须像开发者一样，对如何打造卓越的产品体验了如指掌。但通常他们不得不去督促开发者把事情做到最细微的层面。而未来，无论是再过一两年还是五年，产品经理都将亲自“写代码”——引号里的“写代码”——而不是只填写JIRA工单然后等开发者来处理。开发者将能够专注于人工智能模型无法胜任的智力挑战任务，同时借助模型辅助完成工作。而产品经理则能直接上手进行修改。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to follow that thread, but first of all, I want to also add, and correct me if you disagree with this. I think when we talk about PMs, that also applies to founders, like product thinking founders-
turns.zh: 我想接着谈这个话题，但首先我还要补充一点，如果你们不同意我的观点请随时纠正。我认为当我们谈到产品经理时，这同样适用于创始人，比如具备产品思维的创始人——

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: One hundred percent.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... very similar. And then, I think it's also important to note, if you also have engineering skills and design skills, you will be at an advantage. That only helps you. But if you're looking at this triangle of the triad of product, engineering, PM, it feels like the PME skills are the ones that will be most important and valuable. Although it'd be great if you can also be in code, and if you could also design really well.
turns.zh: ……非常相似。然后，我认为还有一点很重要，如果你同时具备工程技能和设计技能，那你将占据优势。这只会对你有所助益。但如果你审视产品、工程、产品经理这三者的三角关系，就会发现产品经理、设计师和非技术型创业者的技能将成为最重要、最有价值的。不过如果你还能编写代码、设计得很好，那当然更好了。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Absolutely. And to me, it's the most exciting mix. I think PMs, designers and entrepreneurs that are non-technical, that's the most exciting thing to me, just because it's a brand new market that's being unlocked here. For the first time ever, these folks can directly code and build the product, themselves. Their vision, directly into the software itself. That's going to change everything. That is changing everything.
turns.zh: 绝对没错。对我来说，这是最激动人心的组合。我认为产品经理、设计师和非技术型创业者——这才是最让我兴奋的，因为这是一个全新的市场正在被开启。这些人第一次能够直接编写代码、亲自构建产品。他们的愿景能够直接融入软件本身。这将改变一切。真的会彻底改变一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So when you talk about how org charts are going to change, what are you imagining there? Is it just fewer engineers, mostly, or what do the future org charts look like?
turns.zh: 那么当你谈到组织结构会发生变化时，你想象中的样子是怎样的？主要是工程师数量减少吗？还是未来的组织结构会是什么样子？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Good question. And I bet you there's going to be some Gartner analysis someday, years from now or whatever that's like, "Here's how the best," some term is applied to how the best companies are organizing. But yeah, I think that we're going to see developers probably being pulled off of a lot of the, generally speaking, pulled off of a lot of user interface type work. I would imagine. Except for the most complicated of those things. And you're going to see designers and PMs really, really leading the charge, and being responsible for crafting those experiences. And perhaps having a developer attached to be reviewing the code and making sure the guiding, the code that they're writing, reviewing those pull requests and et cetera. And I think maybe even the engineers are... Like you pointed out, having engineering skills is not going to hurt you. It's going to make you way more effective. (00:58:58): But I do think there's going to be, the leverage that the front engineer is going to have is, it is now insane, it's only going to get more so. And so I could see there just being fewer front engineers attached to, I'm seeing more product and design folks, with one or two engineers or something. And really having a larger matching of pods like that. Something like that strikes me as probably how this is going to start trending towards.
turns.zh:
问得好。说不定未来几年，Gartner会出个分析报告，探讨“顶尖公司如何组织架构”之类的内容。但我觉得，我们会看到开发者逐渐从用户界面相关的工作中解放出来——至少最复杂的部分除外。届时，设计师和产品经理将真正主导产品体验的打造，而开发者则负责代码审查，确保代码质量符合规范，处理拉取请求等工作。工程技能无疑会提升效率，这一点毋庸置疑。

（00:58:58）：我认为前端工程师的价值将被进一步放大——这种趋势已然势不可挡。未来团队可能只会配备1-2名工程师，而产品和设计团队将成为核心角色。这种职能匹配的趋势值得关注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on, we had a researcher from OpenAI in the podcast. She actually started her career, she worked at Anthropic first, as a front-end engineer. And said that once she saw what Clyde could do, for front-end engineering, she's like, "I need to move to a different function." And so she moved into research, because she saw that role disappearing, potentially. And that's exactly what you're saying.
turns.zh: 这让我想到，我们播客中曾邀请过OpenAI的研究员。她最初在Anthropic担任前端工程师，后来发现Clyde（AI模型）能替代前端工程任务后，便转入研究领域，因为她预见前端工程岗位或将消失。这与你的观点不谋而合。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let me ask you this, I don't know if you have a clear thesis on this yet, but say, you just had a kid. Say your kid is, in the future, starting school. Let's say your kid was starting college soon. Do you have thoughts on just what skills slash areas you think they should go into, versus avoid, that maybe are popular now and are going to be less popular?
turns.zh: 那么我想问，你是否对此有清晰的判断？假设你刚有孩子，未来孩子要上学了，甚至即将上大学。你认为他们应该掌握哪些技能或领域？哪些热门领域未来可能走向衰落？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Understanding how to leverage these AI tools is key. I wouldn't necessarily, I think maybe getting a basic understanding of how programming works, et cetera, is great.
turns.zh: 掌握AI工具的应用至关重要。但不必拘泥于此，比如掌握编程基础知识还是很有必要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like technical foundations, just understanding how systems work, how coding works.
turns.zh: 比如技术基础，比如理解系统运作原理和编程逻辑。

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Exactly. But it doesn't have to be, because I think back to if Bolt existed, like Albert and I say this to each other all the time. Since the get-go, StackBlitz, we've been building the thing that we wish we had when we were 13. And heck, for everything we built since then. And especially with Bolt. I mean, I don't know if I would've gone as deep as I did on learning how to code, and being an engineer, if that had been around then. The whole reason we got into it is we had ideas for products, and businesses, that we wanted to build. And coding was just a necessary requirement in order to do that. (01:01:21): And that said, I think people need to follow their intrinsic interests. If folks are really interested in really getting in the nitty-gritty of how computers work, and program leaders, or spark and compilers, or whatever, go for it. I think that stuff is still going to be relevant. I don't know if we're going to really have, we'll see, but to the degree that there's AGI where it's like, we don't have to think about anything ever again.
turns.zh: 没错。但其实不必如此，因为我回想起来，如果当时有Bolt这样的工具，比如阿尔伯特和我经常这么说。从一开始创建StackBlitz的时候，我们就一直在打造那些我们13岁时就渴望拥有的产品和业务。尤其是Bolt这款工具。我不确定如果当时就有这样的工具，我是否会像现在这样深入学习编程、成为工程师。我们之所以投身这个领域，是因为我们有想打造的产品和业务，而编程只是实现这些目标的必要条件。（01:01:21）说到这里，我认为人们应该追随自己的内在兴趣。如果有人真的想深入研究计算机的工作原理、编程语言、编译器之类的东西，那就去吧。我觉得这些技术未来依然有用处。我不知道未来是否会真的出现通用人工智能（AGI），但即便有了，我们也不必再操心任何事情了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's always the answer here. Do we sell anything?
turns.zh: 是啊，这里的答案总是如此。我们卖东西吗？

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Yeah, it's like if we're at that point, it's kind of... I don't know, I'm not sure. But I think from, at least what I feel like seems like the next at least five years of what we're looking at, I think people are still going to, there's still going to be places to specialize, and really go deep. But I think you want to go into it with the idea, not like, "I'm going to go and learn computer science because I'm going to get a job for sure out of it." (01:02:18): I just think that's generally not a good... This is like, my co-founder and I, we didn't go to college. My co-founder dropped out of college after a semester or something, but I didn't go, because I was like, "We're coding," we were doing contracting at the time, making money. And it was like, "This is a lot of," you know, it would've been like a hundred grand of debt by the end of the thing, just for four years of in-state tuition, at U of I. 120 grand, I think, at that time. (01:02:49): And lo and behold, I mean there's a huge issue with this. Where people are kind of... There was a prevailing thought by society that going to college in the early 2010s or late two 2000s, that you're going to get a job on the other side. That's going to be high paying. And that just has not been the case for a lot of people. And I think that's just going to continue to be the case. But again, not to deter people from doing it, but you have to go into it being like, "I for sure, this is what I want, and I want to go and be the best that I can possibly be at this thing." You know what I mean?
turns.zh: 是啊，就算到了那一步，也挺……我也不确定。但至少在未来五年内，我们认为人们还是会继续深耕某些领域。但你得带着正确的心态去做这件事，不能抱着“学了计算机科学就能找到工作”的想法。（01:02:18）我觉得这通常不是个好主意……我和我的联合创始人没上过大学。他上了一个学期就退学了，而我甚至没去上大学，因为我当时想，“我们在写代码啊”，当时我们接承包项目赚钱。学费的话，伊利诺伊大学的州内学费加上生活费，一共要12万美元。（01:02:49）果然，现在这个问题很严重。2010年代初到2000年代末，社会普遍认为上大学就能找到高薪工作。但对很多人来说，这根本行不通。我觉得这种情况还会持续下去。不过我不是想劝阻人们不要上大学，而是你必须带着这样的心态去：“我一定要做到最好，成为这方面的顶尖人物。” 你懂我的意思吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like the transfer to your kid is going to be like, "Don't even go to college," potentially.
turns.zh: 我觉得你跟你孩子说起来，可能会说：“别上大学了。”

turns.speaker: Eric Simons
turns.en: Only if they want to. I think at 18, it's a huge ask. I mean, it's a huge ask, not even at 18. It's like at 17, because you could go apply for colleges. It's just such a huge... Like, a six figure debt commitment to someone who's making $0, or negative dollars, and that young. Unless you really have conviction, it costs nothing to go and explore and learn for free, online.
turns.zh: 只要他们想上就行。18岁就去申请大学，这要求太高了。即便不是18岁，17岁去申请也太早了。因为你申请大学的时候，可能连一份工作都找不到。除非你有坚定的信念，否则免费在线学习完全没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to the skills that you think are going to be most important, and let me try to mirror back a few things you said, that I very much agree with. (01:04:11): So it feels like if you want to be successful in the world where AI can build things for you, more and more, what I'm hearing is get good at figuring out what people need and want, what problems they need solved. Get good at articulating it really well to the AI tools. And there's this talk, "You don't need to be a great prompt engineer. You don't need to work on prompting," but it feels like it's more and more important, because you tell it something and it goes off and builds a thing. If you're clear about it, it'll save you a lot of time. (01:04:42): So it's be good at figuring out problems people need solved, figure out how to articulate that problem well, and ask for a clear solution. Figure out how to grow the thing, feels like that's still going to be a need, because Bolt's not going to go and find every... I could see that still running paid ads, and stuff like that. But it feels like that's going to be ongoing need. (01:05:03): And then I feel like there's this kind of unstuck step, like helping AI get unstuck, and it feels like that's where maybe engineering skills will come in more and more. Thoughts on just that skill?

At the time, AOL was trying to reinvigorate the company and they were like, "Hey, we should get young startup blood in here, so let's rent out office space to teenagers," basically. (01:24:24): So I was there, and we ended up running out of money. 20 grand doesn't go very far in the Valley, so three or four months in, we were like, "Oh God, what do we do?"
